name: Freya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for speaking with me, Freya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and your answers are confidential. What do you do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker for the electricity company on the coast, covering the peninsula and the fishing villages. It's overhead lines mostly, and a lot of storm work, because the wind off the sea eats everything. I'm nearly two years in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the weather and my work orders on my phone over breakfast, and I usually ask my AI assistant to quiz me on a section of the regs while I drive to the depot in Harlow Bay. Then it's out with Duncan and the crew, changing salt-crusted insulators, replacing poles, or patching lines the gales took down. I'm not quick on the pole yet, Duncan says I'm all brains and no legs, but I'm getting there. I love storm nights, honestly, the whole village dark and us bringing it back. What wears me out is the salt, it gets into everything, your tools, your hair, your truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least we found out. Some of it's useful, I'll keep using what works. People who sat around waiting for a miracle should get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a bit disappointing, because I had plans that used it. But my job's safe, the sea's not going to stop wrecking lines. And I can still build what I want to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, finish my ticket, and keep looking after my rental house. I'd keep using AI for my bookkeeping and study. In a few years I'd still like to start my own small line contracting firm for the private jobs out here, farms, the marina, holiday parks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the rental house.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought a little two-bedroom in Harlow Bay when I was 25, with my savings and some help from my gran. I rent it to a teacher and I live with Callum, my boyfriend, who fishes. Between the rent and my pay, I've got more than a year of money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's a lot of small private work out here and the company doesn't want it. My dad always said work for yourself if you can, nobody looks after you like you do. I'd need my ticket and a few more years first, though.

S0.say: Freya would say at least people found out, she'd keep using what works, and those waiting for a miracle should get back to work.
S0.think: Privately she'd be slightly disappointed because her plans used AI, but her job is safe with the sea constantly damaging lines. She can still build what she wants.
S0.do: Finishes her ticket, manages her rental house and keeps using AI for bookkeeping and study. Plans to start a small line contracting firm for private coastal work in a few years.
S0.quote: My dad always said work for yourself if you can, nobody looks after you like you do.
S0.fieldNote: Freya combines a self-reliant, free-market outlook with daily AI use. At 25 she bought a rental house, which shows her drive and planning. Her long-term goal is her own firm, and she isn't waiting for anyone to offer it to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for anyone willing to work at it. The tools will make us faster and safer, and lazy companies will fall behind. I'd say it at the depot and probably on my socials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's great for me. Drones for patrols after storms, AI to plan crews, maybe robot arms for the dangerous live work. I'd learn all of it, and it'd make my future firm cheaper to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to let me be on the first drone team, and if they said no, I'd get the licence myself. I'd start using AI to price small private jobs and run the paperwork, so when I go out on my own it's ready. I'd probably put some of the rental income into a second-hand drone this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and keen. Like the first warm day of spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Duncan, probably, and he's the best climber I know. He hates his phone, he still calls me instead of texting. I'd want to help him, but he's proud, so I'd have to be sneaky about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help people who struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training, sure, apprenticeships. But I don't want people paid to sit at home. Around here, the community looks after its own, the lifeboat crew, the church, everyone.

S1.say: Freya would say steady change is good for anyone willing to work at it, making crews faster and safer while lazy companies fall behind. She'd say it at work and on social media.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it's great for her: drones, AI crew planning and robot arms for live work, all of which would also make her future firm cheaper to run.
S1.do: Asks to join the first drone team or gets the licence herself. Uses AI to price small jobs and handle paperwork in preparation for her own firm, and buys a second-hand drone with rental income this year.
S1.feel: Calm and keen, like the first warm day of spring.
S1.quote: He hates his phone, he still calls me instead of texting.
S1.fieldNote: Freya treats steady change as a business opportunity and prepares her future firm early. She supports training and apprenticeships but rejects being paid to stay home. Her soft spot for her proud mentor showed a gentler side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shake-up and people need to get moving, not sit and wait for the government. There'll be winners and losers, and the ones who move first will do better. I'd also say the community has to look after the people who get hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say. I could see myself running robot crews and doing well. But two years is fast, and Callum's fishing could go to robot boats, and the whole village could empty out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the slow plan and go straight for it: set up my small firm within the year and buy or lease whatever robots and drones the private jobs needed. I'd use the rental house as security for a loan if I had to. And I'd learn every system that came out, the week it came out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited for me, worried for the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Using the rental house as security is a big risk. Why take it with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything changes in two years, the people who own the machines are the ones who'll be all right. I'd rather risk the house on that than sit and watch it lose value. Gran would understand, she was the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should come and work with me. Somebody has to run the drones at sea and fix the robots on the boats. He'd say no at first, he always does.

S2.say: Freya would say people need to move rather than wait for government, with first movers doing best. She'd add that the community must look after those hit hardest.
S2.think: Privately it worries her more than she'd admit: she could run robot crews, but the speed threatens her partner's fishing and could empty the village.
S2.do: Starts her own firm within the year, buying or leasing robots and drones for private jobs, using the rental house as loan security if needed. Learns each new system as soon as it appears.
S2.feel: Uneasy: excited for herself but worried for the village.
S2.quote: I'd rather risk the house on that than sit and watch it lose value. Gran would understand, she was the same.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture accelerates Freya's existing business plan rather than overturning it. She's willing to take real financial risk to own the machines. Her worry is about her partner and her village, which she keeps quieter in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. Learn the machines, plan your next step. I'd tell the young lads at the depot not to waste it on their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this might be the best one for me. I finish my ticket, get three good years on the poles, and set up my firm just as the robots get cheap. I'd be 32 and ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get my drone licence, finish my ticket early if I could, and write a proper business plan with AI's help. I'd save the rental income instead of spending any of it. Around year three I'd leave the company and start the firm with a couple of robots and maybe Duncan, if he'd come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a kick of excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Duncan come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he knows every pole on this peninsula. The robots don't. If I can get him to tell the machines where to go, that's worth more than anything I could buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said in the fast one, the village worries you. What about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, people have time. Callum's already talked about taking a course in marine engineering. Some will still struggle, and we'd help them, that's what villages do.

S3.say: Freya would say five years is plenty for anyone with drive, urging young colleagues to learn the machines and not waste the time on their phones.
S3.think: Privately this may be her best picture: finish her ticket, get three solid years on the poles and launch her firm just as robots become affordable, at 32.
S3.do: Gets a drone licence, aims to finish her ticket early and writes a business plan with AI help, saving all rental income. Leaves the company around year three to start her firm with a few robots and her mentor if he'll join.
S3.feel: Calm, with a kick of excitement.
S3.quote: Because he knows every pole on this peninsula. The robots don't.
S3.fieldNote: Freya's plan is clearest with five years, and she sees experienced workers like her mentor as an asset to pair with robots. Her partner's own retraining eases her worry for the village. Self-reliance and community responsibility sit together in her thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. That sounds harsh, I know. But there'd be time for everyone to find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really comfortable. A full apprenticeship, years of experience, the firm built slowly. Maybe a second rental house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd focus on getting good at the actual climbing, because I'd have time. I'd keep investing the rental income, maybe save toward a second house. I'd start the firm in five or six years, once the robots were proven and cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Very relaxed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said those who waste it only have themselves to blame. Would you include someone like Duncan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's fair, I wouldn't. He's 50-odd, it's different. I mean people my age who just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your life to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm going, Callum with me, maybe kids. A house we own outright. And still going out on storm nights, even if it's just to watch the robots do the climbing.

S4.say: Freya would call ten years a gift and say people who waste it have only themselves to blame, admitting it sounds harsh, while believing there's time for everyone to find something.
S4.think: Privately she'd be very comfortable, with a full apprenticeship, years of experience and time to build the firm slowly, perhaps adding a second rental house.
S4.do: Focuses on her climbing in the first year and invests rental income toward a second house. Plans to start her firm in five or six years once robots are proven and cheap.
S4.quote: And still going out on storm nights, even if it's just to watch the robots do the climbing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Freya slows down and chooses craft first, business later. She softened her harsh line about blame when asked about an older colleague. Her vision of 2036 is about owning things and staying part of the storm-night community.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, not for me but for Callum and the village. What would help is training that's quick and practical, and small-business loans so local people can own the machines instead of some big outfit from the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets to own the robots in places like ours. If it's local people, the money stays in Harlow Bay. If it's not, we're just watching our own work get done by someone else's machines.

headlineQuote: If it's local people, the money stays in Harlow Bay.
portrait: Freya Baker is a 27-year-old junior lineworker on a storm-battered coastal peninsula, still slow on the pole but quick with technology and AI, which she uses daily for study and bookkeeping. She bought a rental house at 25 with help from her gran, lives with her fisherman boyfriend Callum and dreams of her own small contracting firm. She believes in self-reliance, community and apprenticeships over handouts, and sees AI and robots as tools to own rather than threats. She's calm in nearly every picture and only uneasy when AGI arrives in two years, worried for Callum and her village more than herself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, for her partner's fishing and the village rather than for herself.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, practical training and small-business loans so local people can own the machines rather than outside firms.
